whyCorrect: Line the two equations up so one variable cancels. Doubling 3f + 2r = 51 gives 6f + 4r = 102, and the second equation is 5f + 4r = 93; subtracting kills the r terms and leaves f = 9. Put that back into 3f + 2r = 51: 27 + 2r = 51, so 2r = 24 and r = 12.

whyWrong.A: 9 is f, the hours per flue pipe — the value you find first, not the one the question asks for.
whyWrong.C: 15 comes from solving 2r = 51 - 21 or similar arithmetic slip when substituting f = 9 back in; check that 3(9) = 27, not 21.
whyWrong.D: 21 is 51 - 3(10) or the result of eliminating the wrong variable and then dividing by 1 instead of 2; substituting r = 21 into 5f + 4r = 93 gives a negative f.

commonMistakes: Solving the system correctly and then reporting f because it was the variable that fell out first.
tips: Circle the variable the question asks for before you start eliminating.

whyCorrect: The slope is the same everywhere on a line, so use the two known points: \(\frac{11a-3a}{3a-a}=\frac{8a}{2a}=4\) . The a cancels, so the slope is just 4. Going from \((3a,\ 11a)\) to \((7a,\ y)\) the run is 7a - 3a = 4a, so y = 11a + 4(4a) = 27a.

whyWrong.A: 19a mixes the two points: it adds the run measured from one point to the y-value of the other.
whyWrong.B: 23a uses 3a as the run instead of the difference 7a - 3a = 4a.
whyWrong.D: 31a starts at \((a,\ 3a)\) but uses 7a as the whole run, forgetting to subtract the a: the run is 7a - a = 6a, giving 3a + 24a = 27a.

commonMistakes: Treating a as something that has to be solved for; it cancels out of the slope and stays as a factor in the answer.
tips: Once you have the slope, write the line as y = 4x - a and check it against both given points before substituting x = 7a.

whyCorrect: To fit the most reed pipes, build the fewest flue pipes the specification allows, which is exactly twice the reed count: F = 2R. Hours then give 3(2R) + 5R = 11R, and money gives 50(2R) + 160R = 260R. So \(11R\le 240\) forces \(R\le 21.8\) and \(260R\le 6400\) forces \(R\le 24.6\) ; the tighter limit is 21. Checking R = 21, F = 42: 231 hours and $5,460, both within the limits.

whyWrong.A: 12 is well inside both limits — it uses only about 132 hours and $3,120, so it is possible but far from the greatest.
whyWrong.B: 16 is what you get from 240/15 if you charge 5 hours to every pipe; flue pipes take 3 hours, not 5.
whyWrong.C: 18 comes from swapping the two times, using 3 hours for a reed pipe and 5 for each flue pipe (13 hours per group instead of 11).

commonMistakes: Forgetting the flue pipes entirely and dividing 240 by 5 or $6,400 by $160 — the flues that the specification forces you to build are what consume most of the shop time.
tips: When a question asks for the greatest number of one item, set the other item to the smallest amount the constraints allow, then test both limits and take the smaller answer.

whyCorrect: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 2) = 5(x - 4). Distribute both sides fully, giving 3x + 6 = 5x - 20. Subtract 3x and add 20 to both sides: 26 = 2x, so x = 13.

whyWrong.A: 7 comes from a sign slip moving the 6 across: 3x - 5x = -20 + 6 gives -2x = -14 only if the 6 keeps its sign, but moving +6 to the right makes it -6, so the constant is -26.
whyWrong.B: 11 comes from distributing only the first term on the left, writing 3x + 2 instead of 3x + 6.
whyWrong.D: 17 is 13 with the 4 from x - 4 added back on, as if x stood for the denominator rather than for x itself.

commonMistakes: Multiplying only the x terms across and leaving the constants where they are.
tips: Substitute your answer back: with x = 13 both sides are 3/9 = 5/15 = 1/3, which confirms it.

whyCorrect: A linear function changes by the same amount for each unit of x. From x = 2 to x = 6 the output rises by 13a - 5a = 8a over 4 units, so the rate is 2a per unit. From x = 6 to x = 10 is another 4 units, so \(h(10)=13a+8a=21a\) .

whyWrong.A: 17a adds only 4a, as if the input moved 2 units instead of 4.
whyWrong.B: 19a comes from writing h(x) = 2ax + b, finding b = a, and then subtracting it: h(10) = 20a + a, not 20a - a.
whyWrong.D: 26a doubles h(6), which would only work if h were proportional (passing through the origin); this line has y-intercept a, so h(10) is not 2h(6) — and 10 is not twice 6 anyway.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because the inputs 2, 6, 10 are evenly spaced you can jump straight to doubling an output.
tips: Equally spaced inputs give equally spaced outputs for a linear function: 5a, 13a, 21a rises by 8a each time.

whyCorrect: Name the first rank x. The second is x + 12 and the third is 3x - 9, so x + (x + 12) + (3x - 9) = 183. Collect terms: 5x + 3 = 183, so 5x = 180 and x = 36. The third rank has 3(36) - 9 = 99 pipes.
commonMistakes: Solving for x and stopping there, or reading "9 fewer than three times the first" as 3(x - 9).
tips: Check the total: 36 + 48 + 99 = 183.

whyCorrect: Clear both denominators at once by multiplying every term by 6: \(2(2x-5)\le 3(x+4)\) . That is 4x - 10 ≤ 3x + 12. Subtract 3x and add 10: x ≤ 22, so the greatest integer that works is 22.

whyWrong.A: 11 is half of 22 — it comes from dividing by the 2 in the right-hand denominator a second time after it had already been cleared.
whyWrong.B: 17 comes from distributing only partway on the left, writing 4x - 5 instead of 4x - 10.
whyWrong.D: 34 comes from multiplying the 4 on the right by 6 instead of by 3: the 6 cancels the denominator 2 and leaves a factor of 3, so the right side is 3x + 12.

commonMistakes: Multiplying each side by its own denominator only, which leaves fractions behind.
tips: Test the boundary: at x = 22 both sides equal 13, so 22 satisfies the inequality and 23 does not.

whyCorrect: \(f(g(x))\) means put g(x) into f wherever x appears: \((x-3)^{2}+5(x-3)\) . Expand both pieces: \(x^{2}-6x+9\) plus 5x - 15. Combining gives \(x^{2}-x-6\) .

whyWrong.B: \(x^{2}-6x+9\) is only \((x-3)^{2}\) — the 5(x - 3) term was dropped.
whyWrong.C: \(x^{2}+5x-3\) is \(g(f(x))\) , the composition in the other order: it subtracts 3 from f(x) instead of substituting into f.
whyWrong.D: \(x^{2}-11x+24\) comes from subtracting 5(x - 3) instead of adding it.

commonMistakes: Substituting into the squared term but forgetting that the 5x term also becomes 5(x - 3).

whyCorrect: The common denominator is \((x-2)(x+1)=x^{2}-x-2\) , so the first fraction becomes 3(x + 1) over it and the second becomes 2(x - 2) over it. The numerator is therefore 3(x + 1) - 2(x - 2) = 3x + 3 - 2x + 4 = x + 7. Note that subtracting -4 adds 4.

whyWrong.A: x - 7 comes from attaching each numerator to the wrong denominator's constant, giving 3x - 3 and 2x + 4.
whyWrong.C: 5x - 1 is 3(x + 1) + 2(x - 2) — the two numerators added instead of subtracted.
whyWrong.D: 5x + 7 adds the numerators and also flips the sign inside 2(x - 2), doubling the error.

commonMistakes: Distributing the minus sign to only the first term of 2(x - 2).

whyCorrect: For \(x^{2}-16x+k=0\) the two solutions add to 16 and multiply to k. If they differ by 6 and add to 16, they are 11 and 5, since 11 + 5 = 16 and 11 - 5 = 6. Then k is their product, 11(5) = 55.
commonMistakes: Trying to factor by guessing pairs that multiply to an unknown k; the sum and difference pin the roots down directly.
tips: Two numbers with sum S and difference D are \(\frac{S+D}{2}\) and \(\frac{S-D}{2}\) .

whyCorrect: The two frequencies are \(F\left(2^{\frac{19}{12}}\right)\) and \(F\left(2^{\frac{7}{12}}\right)\) . Dividing, the F cancels and you subtract the exponents: \(2^{\frac{19}{12}-\frac{7}{12}}=2^{\frac{12}{12}}=2\) . The two pipes are 12 semitones apart, which is exactly one octave, so the ratio is 2.

whyWrong.B: 4 would mean two octaves, or 24 semitones; the gap here is 19 - 7 = 12 semitones.
whyWrong.C: \(2^{\frac{13}{12}}\) comes from subtracting 19 - 7 as 13.
whyWrong.D: \(2^{\frac{19}{7}}\) divides the exponents instead of subtracting them — dividing powers of the same base subtracts exponents.

commonMistakes: Multiplying or dividing the fractional exponents rather than subtracting.
tips: Any 12-semitone gap in equal temperament doubles the frequency, so you can answer this without touching the exponent arithmetic.

whyCorrect: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents: \(\frac{5}{6}-\frac{1}{3}\) . Rewrite \(\frac{1}{3}\) as \(\frac{2}{6}\) , not \(\frac{3}{6}\) . That leaves \(\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}\) , so the quotient is \(a^{\frac{1}{2}}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(a^{\frac{1}{3}}\) comes from converting \(\frac{1}{3}\) to \(\frac{3}{6}\) instead of \(\frac{2}{6}\) .
whyWrong.C: \(a^{\frac{5}{18}}\) multiplies the exponents, which is the rule for a power of a power, not for a quotient.
whyWrong.D: \(a^{\frac{7}{6}}\) adds the exponents, which is the rule for a product.

commonMistakes: Converting to sixths by multiplying the wrong part of the fraction.

whyCorrect: Substitute y = 2x into the circle: \(x^{2}+(2x)^{2}=45\) , so \(5x^{2}=45\) and \(x^{2}=9\) . The x-coordinates are 3 and -3, and their product is -9.

whyWrong.A: -27 would require x-coordinates like 3 and -9, but the equation \(x^{2}=9\) forces the two values to be opposites of each other.
whyWrong.B: -18 multiplies an x-coordinate by a y-coordinate (3 and -6) instead of multiplying the two x-coordinates.
whyWrong.D: 3 is one x-coordinate, not the product of both — and a product of opposite numbers must be negative.

commonMistakes: Squaring 2x as \(2x^{2}\) instead of \(4x^{2}\) , which changes the equation to \(3x^{2}=45\) .
tips: For \(5x^{2}-45=0\) the product of the roots is \(\frac{-45}{5}=-9\) , so you never have to find the roots individually.

whyCorrect: Mean is total mass over number of bells, and both change. The new total mass is \(m+\frac{3m}{n}=\frac{mn+3m}{n}=\frac{m(n+3)}{n}\) , and the new count is n + 1. Dividing by n + 1 gives \(\frac{m(n+3)}{n(n+1)}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{3m}{n+1}\) divides only the new bell's mass by the new count, ignoring the original m kilograms.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{m+3}{n+1}\) treats the added bell as weighing 3 kilograms rather than \(\frac{3m}{n}\) .
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{m(n+3)}{n}\) is the new total mass; it never gets divided by the n + 1 bells.

commonMistakes: Adding the new mass to the total but forgetting that the count rises from n to n + 1.
tips: Test with numbers: n = 3 bells totalling m = 12 kg, plus a bell of 12 kg, gives 24/4 = 6, and only choice D returns 6.

whyCorrect: "Given that the pipe selected is a reed pipe" restricts you to the reed row, so the denominator is 90, not 330. Of those 90 reed pipes, 63 are tin-rich, so the probability is \(\frac{63}{90}=\frac{7}{10}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{7}{33}\) divides by a whole-table total instead of by the 90 reed pipes.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{10}\) is \(\frac{27}{90}\) , the chance the reed pipe is lead-rich — the complement of what was asked.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{3}{7}\) is \(\frac{63}{147}\) , which conditions on the tin-rich column instead: it answers "given a tin-rich pipe, what is the chance it is a reed pipe?"

commonMistakes: Using 330 as the denominator whenever a table gives a grand total.
tips: The words after "given that" tell you which row or column becomes your entire sample space.

whyCorrect: Two successive rises multiply, so the original fee times 1.08 times 1.05 is $1,701. Since 1.08(1.05) = 1.134, the original fee is 1701/1.134 = $1,500. Check it forward: 1500(1.08) = 1620, and 1620(1.05) = 1701.

whyWrong.B: $1,530 grows to about $1,735 after the two rises, too high; it comes from knocking a single flat 10 percent off $1,701.
whyWrong.C: $1,559 grows to about $1,768 after the two rises — it takes the percentages off the final amount instead of dividing.
whyWrong.D: $1,650 treats the two rises as one net 3 percent rise and removes it; carried forward, $1,650 would become about $1,871.

commonMistakes: Adding 8 and 5 to get a single 13 percent rise; compounding gives 13.4 percent because the second rise applies to the already-raised fee.
tips: To undo a percentage increase, divide by the growth factor — never subtract the same percentage from the new amount.

whyCorrect: Work with totals, not with means. All 30 pipes total 30(48) = 1,440 cm, and the 12 tin-rich pipes total 12(60) = 720 cm. The other 18 pipes therefore total 1440 - 720 = 720 cm, so their mean is 720/18 = 40 cm.

whyWrong.A: 36 divides the remaining 720 cm by 20 rather than by the 18 pipes that are left.
whyWrong.C: 44 fails the check: 12(60) + 18(44) = 1,512 cm, which is a mean of 50.4 cm, not 48.
whyWrong.D: 54 is the midpoint of 48 and 60, and it moves in the wrong direction — since the tin-rich pipes are above the overall mean, the rest must be below 48.

commonMistakes: Averaging the two means directly; that only works when the two groups are the same size.
tips: Convert every mean to a total, do the arithmetic with totals, then convert back at the end.

whyCorrect: The ranks have different sizes, so weight each mean by its number of pipes. The totals are 50(96) = 4,800, 30(60) = 1,800 and 20(30) = 600 centimetres, which sum to 7,200. Dividing by all 100 pipes gives 72 cm.

whyWrong.A: 62 is the plain average of 96, 60 and 30, which would only be right if the three ranks had equal numbers of pipes.
whyWrong.C: 78 is the average of 96 and 60, leaving the 20 Fifteenth pipes out entirely.
whyWrong.D: 95 is essentially the Open Diapason's own mean, as if the two shorter ranks did not pull the overall figure down.

commonMistakes: Averaging the three listed means without weighting.
tips: A weighted mean always lands between the smallest and largest group means and closest to the largest group — here that is the 50-pipe rank.

whyCorrect: \(\tan A=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\) , so you can take the side opposite A to be a and the side adjacent to be b. The hypotenuse is then \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\) by the Pythagorean theorem. Since \(\sin A=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\) , the answer is \(\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{b}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}\) is adjacent over hypotenuse, which is \(\cos A\) .
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{a}{a+b}\) adds the two legs instead of combining them with the Pythagorean theorem; a + b is longer than the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}{a}\) is the reciprocal, hypotenuse over opposite, which is greater than 1 and so cannot be a sine.

commonMistakes: Assuming the hypotenuse is a + b because the triangle's legs are a and b.
tips: A sine is always at most 1, which rules out any choice whose numerator is the hypotenuse.

whyCorrect: Drop a perpendicular from the centre to the chord; it bisects the chord and makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the radius 25 and whose short leg is the distance 20. The half-chord is \(\sqrt{25^{2}-20^{2}}=\sqrt{625-400}=\sqrt{225}=15\) . The full chord is twice that, 30 cm.

whyWrong.A: 12 fails the check: half of it is 6, and \(6^{2}+20^{2}=436\) , not \(25^{2}=625\) .
whyWrong.B: 20 repeats the distance from the centre rather than computing the chord.
whyWrong.C: 24 gives a half-chord of 12, and \(12^{2}+20^{2}=544\) , which is not 625 either.

commonMistakes: Finding the half-chord of 15 and reporting it, or subtracting 25 - 20 instead of using the Pythagorean theorem.
tips: The perpendicular from the centre always bisects the chord, so whatever leg you compute has to be doubled.

whyCorrect: With no ends, the metal is just the curved surface, \(2\pi rL\) . The second pipe has radius 2r and length \(\frac{L}{2}\) , so its area is \(2\pi(2r)\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)=2\pi rL\) . The doubling and the halving cancel exactly, so the ratio is 1.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{2}\) applies the halved length but not the doubled radius.
whyWrong.C: 2 applies the doubled radius but not the halved length.
whyWrong.D: 4 squares the radius change, which is the rule for areas of similar figures scaled in every direction — here only the radius doubles while the length shrinks.

commonMistakes: Using \(2\pi r^{2}+2\pi rL\) , the closed-cylinder formula, when the problem says there is no metal at either end.
tips: Curved surface area is linear in both r and L, so a factor of 2 on one and \(\frac{1}{2}\) on the other leaves it unchanged.

whyCorrect: The small cone cut off at the midpoint of the axis is similar to the whole cone, with every length half as big — half the height and half the base radius. Volume scales with the cube of the linear ratio, so the small cone has \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=\frac{1}{8}\) of the volume. You can confirm with the formula: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi\left(\frac{r}{2}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{h}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{8}\left(\frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h\right)\) .
commonMistakes: Answering 1/2 because the cut is at the midpoint, or 1/4 by scaling only the base area.
tips: Halving every dimension of any solid divides the volume by 8, never by 2.

whyCorrect: Let x be the mass from each of the six equal pans. The seventh gave x - 140, so 6x + (x - 140) = 4060. That is 7x - 140 = 4060, so 7x = 4200 and x = 600 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 560 comes from subtracting the 140 before dividing: (4060 - 140)/7. The 140 has to be added back, because the total is short by that amount.
whyWrong.B: 580 is 4060/7, which splits the total evenly and ignores that one pan gave less than the others.
whyWrong.D: 620 adds the 140 twice, dividing 4340 by 7.

commonMistakes: Deciding whether the missing 140 kilograms should be added or subtracted before dividing.
tips: Check the total: 6(600) + 460 = 4,060.

whyCorrect: Let T be the mass stored at the start. After 260 tonnes came out, \(T-260=\frac{3}{5}T\) . Subtract \(\frac{3}{5}T\) from both sides: \(\frac{2}{5}T=260\) . So the 260 tonnes taken out are two fifths of the original, and \(T=260\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=650\) tonnes.

whyWrong.A: 390 is \(\frac{3}{5}\) of 650 — the mass still stored, not the mass stored before any was taken out.
whyWrong.B: 520 doubles the 260, which would be right only if the 260 tonnes were half the original store.
whyWrong.D: 780 triples the 260, treating the amount removed as one third of the original.

commonMistakes: Taking three fifths of 260 instead of recognising 260 as the remaining two fifths.
tips: When a fraction is left, the part removed is the rest of the whole: 1 - 3/5 = 2/5.

whyCorrect: The second pan gives 24d + 16 kilograms after d days. Set the two expressions equal: 18d + 40 = 24d + 16. Subtract 18d and 16 from both sides to get 24 = 6d, so d = 4. Both pans have then given 112 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 3 days leaves the first pan at 94 kilograms and the second at 88 — not yet equal.
whyWrong.C: 6 days is past the crossing point: the first pan is at 148 kilograms and the faster second pan has pulled ahead to 160.
whyWrong.D: 8 days puts the pans at 184 and 208 kilograms, further apart still.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the rates and the starting amounts in opposite orders, which flips the sign of d.
tips: The second pan starts 24 kilograms behind and gains 6 kilograms a day, so it needs 24/6 = 4 days to catch up.

whyCorrect: The rate is the slope: (132 - 186)/(26 - 8) = -54/18 = -3 tonnes per day. Writing the model from the day-8 reading, M = 186 - 3(d - 8) = 210 - 3d. Setting 210 - 3d = 0 gives d = 70, so the store is empty on day 70.

whyWrong.A: 62 is the number of further days after day 8, not the day of the summer; you still have to add the 8.
whyWrong.B: 64 leaves 210 - 3(64) = 18 tonnes still in the store, so the ice has not run out.
whyWrong.D: 74 gives 210 - 3(74) = -12, meaning the store emptied four days earlier.

commonMistakes: Finding how long the ice lasts from a given reading and forgetting that the question asks for a day number on the summer's calendar.
tips: Turn two readings into the full equation M = 210 - 3d first; then every follow-up question is one substitution.

whyCorrect: Profit is revenue minus both kinds of cost: 2.40b - 0.35b - 560, which is 2.05b - 560. Setting \(2.05b-560\ge 900\) gives \(2.05b\ge 1460\) and \(b\ge 712.19\) . Bushels are whole, and 712 gives only $899.60 of profit, so 713 is the least number that works.

whyWrong.A: 685 bushels earn 685(2.05) - 560 = $844.25 of profit, short of the $900 target.
whyWrong.C: 720 does clear $900 (it gives $916), but it is not the least such number — 713 already works.
whyWrong.D: 736 gives $948.80, further past the target than necessary.

commonMistakes: Dividing 900 by 2.05 and forgetting that the 560 pounds of fixed cost must be earned back first.
tips: When an inequality with a whole-number answer comes out to 712.19, test 712 as well as 713 rather than assuming which way to round.

whyCorrect: The original mass is M at w = 0, which is 310 tonnes, so 15 percent of it is 46.5 tonnes. You need \(310-4.6w\le 46.5\) , which gives \(4.6w\ge 263.5\) and \(w\ge 57.28\) . Since the store is swept after a whole number of weeks, that is week 58.

whyWrong.A: 47 is close to the 46.5-tonne threshold; that figure is a mass, not a number of weeks.
whyWrong.B: 52 weeks leaves 310 - 4.6(52) = 70.8 tonnes, about 23 percent of the original — still too much.
whyWrong.C: 57 is 57.28 rounded down, but at 57 weeks 47.8 tonnes remain, which is still above the 46.5-tonne limit; with a "no more than" condition you must round up.

commonMistakes: Taking 15 percent of the current mass instead of the original 310 tonnes.
tips: After solving an inequality, substitute the two whole numbers on either side of your answer and see which one actually satisfies the condition.

whyCorrect: Let L be the number of large blocks; the small blocks number 96 - L. Their masses give 42L + 26(96 - L) = 3232, which is 16L + 2496 = 3232. So 16L = 736 and L = 46 large blocks (and 50 small ones).
commonMistakes: Solving for the small blocks and reporting that number, or dividing 3,232 by 42.
tips: Check both conditions: 46 + 50 = 96 blocks and 42(46) + 26(50) = 3,232 kilograms.

whyCorrect: Multiply every term of the first factor by every term of the second: \(5p(2p)=10p^{2}\) , \(5p(-3)=-15p\) , \(6(2p)=12p\) and \(6(-3)=-18\) . The two middle terms combine as -15p + 12p = -3p, giving \(10p^{2}-3p-18\) .

whyWrong.B: \(10p^{2}+3p-18\) combines the middle terms as +15p - 12p, reversing which product is negative.
whyWrong.C: \(10p^{2}-3p+18\) has the right middle term but multiplies 6 by -3 as +18.
whyWrong.D: \(10p^{2}+27p-18\) adds the middle terms as 15p + 12p, ignoring the minus sign on the 3.

commonMistakes: Losing track of the minus sign in 2p - 3, which affects both the middle term and the constant.
tips: Check with p = 1: the original is 11(-1) = -11, and \(10-3-18=-11\) .

whyCorrect: Split the radicand into perfect squares and what is left: \(72n^{5}=36\cdot 2\cdot n^{4}\cdot n\) . The square root of 36 is 6 and the square root of \(n^{4}\) is \(n^{2}\) , so those come out; the 2 and the single n have no square factor and stay in. That gives \(6n^{2}\sqrt{2n}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(6n^{2}\sqrt{2}\) loses the leftover n: \(n^{5}\) is an odd power, so one factor of n must remain under the radical.
whyWrong.C: \(36n^{2}\sqrt{2n}\) brings the 36 out without taking its square root.
whyWrong.D: \(6n^{3}\sqrt{2}\) halves the exponent 5 up to 3 instead of down to 2 and drops the leftover n.

commonMistakes: Treating \(\sqrt{n^{5}}\) as \(n^{3}\) rather than \(n^{2}\sqrt{n}\) .
tips: Test n = 1: the rule gives \(\sqrt{72}=6\sqrt{2}\) , and only a choice that returns \(6\sqrt{2}\) at n = 1 can be right.

whyCorrect: Take the square root of both sides, remembering both signs: 2x - 7 = 9 or 2x - 7 = -9. The first gives 2x = 16 and x = 8; the second gives 2x = -2 and x = -1. The positive solution is 8.

whyWrong.A: 4 divides by 2 a second time after x = 8 has already been found; \((2\cdot 4-7)^{2}=1\) , not 81.
whyWrong.C: 11 applies the 7 to the 9 without accounting for the coefficient 2: \((2\cdot 11-7)^{2}=225\) .
whyWrong.D: 16 stops at 2x = 16 without dividing by 2.

commonMistakes: Expanding \((2x-7)^{2}\) into a quadratic when taking the square root of both sides is far quicker.
tips: A squared expression equal to a number always has two cases; check which one the question asks for.

whyCorrect: The second week runs from w = 1 to w = 2, so you need those two values, not the starting amount. \(T(1)=240\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)=180\) and \(T(2)=240\left(\frac{9}{16}\right)=135\) . The loss during the second week alone is 180 - 135 = 45 tonnes.

whyWrong.B: 60 is the loss during the first week, from 240 down to 180.
whyWrong.C: 75 matches no pair of the model's values, which are 240, 180 and 135 tonnes at w = 0, 1 and 2.
whyWrong.D: 105 is the total lost over both weeks, 240 - 135.

commonMistakes: Assuming an exponential model loses the same amount each week; it loses the same fraction, so each week's loss is smaller than the last.
tips: For a "during the nth period" question, evaluate the model at both ends of that period and subtract.

whyCorrect: As h grows, \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{h}\) shrinks towards 0, so the term \(8\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{h}\) fades away and T(h) approaches 11 - 0 = 11 degrees. That constant 11 is the horizontal asymptote: the temperature the ice house is warming towards but never quite reaches.

whyWrong.A: 3 is T(0) = 11 - 8, the temperature at the moment the door is opened, not the long-run value.
whyWrong.B: 8 is the coefficient that measures how far below 11 the temperature starts; it is a gap, not a temperature.
whyWrong.D: 19 is 11 + 8, which would be the limit only if the exponential term were added rather than subtracted — the temperature rises towards 11 from below.

commonMistakes: Reading the number attached to the exponential as the answer instead of the constant it is subtracted from.
tips: In \(a+b\cdot r^{h}\) with \(0<r<1\) , the long-run value is always a.

whyCorrect: You need \(-s^{2}+22s-40>0\) , which is the same as \(s^{2}-22s+40<0\) . The roots of \(s^{2}-22s+40=0\) are \(\frac{22\pm\sqrt{484-160}}{2}=\frac{22\pm 18}{2}\) , that is 2 and 20. An upward parabola is below zero strictly between its roots, so B(s) is positive for 2 < s < 20, and the greatest whole number of sawyers is 19.
commonMistakes: Answering 20, which is a root and gives exactly 0 blocks — not a positive number.

whyCorrect: Percentage lost is the tonnage lost divided by the tonnage cut in, so compute each one: Ashwell 84/480 = 17.5 percent, Barrow 49/350 = 14 percent, Cranford 124/620 = 20 percent, Deeping 81/540 = 15 percent. Cranford lost the greatest share.

whyWrong.A: Ashwell lost 17.5 percent, the second highest but not the greatest.
whyWrong.B: Barrow lost the least, both in tonnes (49) and as a share (14 percent).
whyWrong.D: Deeping lost 81 tonnes of 540, which is 15 percent.

commonMistakes: Comparing the delivered tonnages, or the losses in tonnes, without dividing by the very different amounts each house started with.
tips: With four rows this size, work out each ratio as a decimal rather than trying to compare fractions by eye.

whyCorrect: The column gives running totals, not weekly amounts, so the third week alone is the change from the end of week 2 to the end of week 3: 305 - 214 = 91 tonnes.

whyWrong.A: 67 is the fourth week's amount, 372 - 305.
whyWrong.C: 118 is the second week's amount, 214 - 96.
whyWrong.D: 305 is the running total through the end of the third week, which includes weeks 1 and 2.

commonMistakes: Reading a cumulative table as though each row were that period's own figure.
tips: Check the header wording: "total cut in by the end of the week" means you must subtract consecutive rows to get one week's work.

whyCorrect: One block has volume 0.5(0.4)(0.3) = 0.06 cubic metre, so its mass is 0.06(920) = 55.2 kilograms. Dividing the limit by that, 1150/55.2 = 20.83, and blocks are whole, so the sledge can take 20.

whyWrong.A: 18 blocks weigh 993.6 kilograms — within the limit, but not the greatest number that fits.
whyWrong.B: 19 blocks weigh 1,048.8 kilograms, still leaving room for another block.
whyWrong.D: 21 blocks weigh 1,159.2 kilograms, which is over the 1,150-kilogram limit; 20.83 must be rounded down here.

commonMistakes: Adding the three dimensions instead of multiplying them, or rounding 20.83 up because that is the usual habit.
tips: With a "at most" limit, always round down and then check the load: 20 blocks come to 1,104 kilograms.

whyCorrect: Range is the largest reading minus the smallest. Millpond: 21 - 13 = 8. Nether Pond: 18 - 16 = 2. The Millpond range is 8 - 2 = 6 centimetres greater.

whyWrong.A: 2 is the Nether Pond range on its own, not the difference between the two ranges.
whyWrong.B: 4 is neither range (8 and 2) nor the gap between them (6); it comes from comparing only part of each set.
whyWrong.D: 8 is the Millpond range on its own.

commonMistakes: Being distracted by the equal means; the means are equal precisely so that only the spread distinguishes the ponds.
tips: Range uses only two numbers from each list — find the largest and smallest first and ignore the rest.

whyCorrect: The salt required rises from 1,472 to 1,840 tonnes, a factor of 1840/1472 = 1.25. At the same yield the water must rise by the same factor, so 46,000(1.25) = 57,500 cubic metres. Equivalently, each tonne needs 46000/1472 = 31.25 cubic metres, and 1840(31.25) = 57,500.

whyWrong.A: 46,000 is the water already used for the smaller amount of salt; more salt needs more water.
whyWrong.B: 51,750 is 46,000 increased by 12.5 percent, half the increase actually needed.
whyWrong.C: 55,200 is 46,000 increased by 20 percent, which takes the extra 368 tonnes as a share of the new total 1,840 instead of the original 1,472.

commonMistakes: Computing the percentage increase against the wrong base — the increase is measured from the old amount.
tips: Set up the proportion 1472/46000 = 1840/x and cross-multiply; it removes the choice of base entirely.

whyCorrect: The sand forms a rectangular slab whose volume is floor area times depth. The floor area is 4.5(3.2) = 14.4 square metres, so the depth is 2.16/14.4 = 0.15 metre.

whyWrong.A: 0.12 divides 2.16 by 18 rather than by the floor area of 14.4.
whyWrong.C: 0.18 divides 2.16 by 12, again not the floor area.
whyWrong.D: 0.24 divides 2.16 by 4.5 and then by 2, using only one side of the floor.

commonMistakes: Dividing by one side length instead of by the product of both.
tips: Check the answer forward: 14.4(0.15) = 2.16 cubic metres.

whyCorrect: Put the corner at the origin of a 16-by-16 square. A side that does not meet that corner is a far side, and its midpoint is 16 across and 8 along. The partition is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 16 and 8, so its length is \(\sqrt{16^{2}+8^{2}}=\sqrt{256+64}=\sqrt{320}=8\sqrt{5}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(4\sqrt{5}\) is \(\sqrt{80}\) , which uses legs of 8 and 4 — both halved.
whyWrong.C: \(8\sqrt{3}\) is \(\sqrt{192}\) , from subtracting \(8^{2}\) from \(16^{2}\) instead of adding.
whyWrong.D: 20 is the hypotenuse of a 12-16-20 triangle, which would need the second leg to be 12 rather than half of 16.

commonMistakes: Taking the midpoint of an adjacent side, which gives legs of 16 and 8 only if you measure across the full square; sketching it settles which leg is 8.
tips: \(\sqrt{320}\) simplifies because \(320=64\cdot 5\) , so the answer is \(8\sqrt{5}\) , about 17.9 metres — longer than a side and shorter than the 22.6-metre diagonal, as it must be.

whyCorrect: The walk is the ring between two circles: the outer one has radius 12 + w and the inner one 12. Its area is \(\pi(12+w)^{2}-\pi(12)^{2}=52\pi\) , so dividing by \(\pi\) gives \((12+w)^{2}-144=52\) . Then \((12+w)^{2}=196\) , so 12 + w = 14 and w = 2 metres.
commonMistakes: Setting \(\pi w^{2}=52\pi\) , which treats the walk as a disc of radius w rather than as a ring around the pan.
tips: Dividing through by \(\pi\) at the first opportunity keeps the numbers small.

whyCorrect: The two legs meet at the right angle C, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(AC)(BC)\) . With BC = 8 and area 60, \(\frac{1}{2}(AC)(8)=60\) gives AC = 15. From angle A, the opposite leg is BC = 8 and the adjacent leg is AC = 15, so \(\tan A=\frac{8}{15}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{15}{8}\) is adjacent over opposite, which is \(\tan B\) , not \(\tan A\) .
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{8}{17}\) uses the hypotenuse 17 as the denominator, making it \(\sin A\) .
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{15}{17}\) is adjacent over hypotenuse, which is \(\cos A\) .

commonMistakes: Finding the third side with the Pythagorean theorem and then using it in a tangent, which never involves the hypotenuse.
tips: Label the sides from the named angle's point of view before choosing the ratio.

whyCorrect: Substitute h = 9 into the expression: 340 - 12(9). Multiply first, then subtract: 12(9) = 108, and 340 - 108 = 232 herring still hanging.

whyWrong.A: 108 is 12(9), the number taken down, not the number left.
whyWrong.B: 196 comes from subtracting 12(12) instead of 12(9).
whyWrong.D: 268 is 340 - 72, which multiplies 12 by 6 rather than by 9.

commonMistakes: Subtracting before multiplying, or answering with the amount removed.
tips: The constant 340 is the starting count and the 12h is what has come down, so the answer must be smaller than 340 but well above 108.

whyCorrect: The 4 left over were never boxed, so 236 - 4 = 232 herring went into full boxes. Each box holds 8, so the curer packed 232/8 = 29 boxes.

whyWrong.A: 24 boxes hold only 192 herring, leaving 44 over — enough for five more full boxes.
whyWrong.B: 27 boxes hold 216 herring, leaving 20 over.
whyWrong.C: 28 boxes hold 224 herring, leaving 12 over; since 12 is more than 8, one more full box could still be packed.

commonMistakes: Dividing 236 by 8 and rounding, instead of removing the 4 left over first.
tips: Check by rebuilding the total: 29(8) + 4 = 236.

whyCorrect: Each row holds 9 wheels and every row is filled, so the number of rows is 153/9. Dividing gives 17 rows, and 17(9) = 153 exactly, so no partial row is needed.
commonMistakes: Multiplying 153 by 9 instead of dividing.
tips: If the division had left a remainder, you would need one extra row; here it comes out even.

whyCorrect: Put w = 12 into m = 4.6 - 0.05w. The loss is 0.05(12) = 0.6 kilogram, so m = 4.6 - 0.6 = 4.0 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 3.4 subtracts 1.2, which uses a loss of 0.1 kilogram a week rather than 0.05.
whyWrong.B: 3.8 subtracts 0.8, a slip in the product 0.05(12).
whyWrong.D: 4.6 is the mass at w = 0, before any time in the cave.

commonMistakes: Misplacing the decimal point in 0.05(12) and getting 6 or 0.06.
tips: 0.05 is a twentieth, so 12 weeks costs 12/20 = 0.6 kilogram.

whyCorrect: Set r = 0, the case with no extra rails fitted: the expression becomes 6(0) + 24 = 24. So the 24 is the number of herring the smokehouse hangs before anything is added — the starting amount that does not depend on r.

whyWrong.B: That describes the 6, the coefficient of r: each extra rail adds 6 herring.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the expression caps the number of rails; 24 is a count of herring, not of rails.
whyWrong.D: The expression adds as r grows, so no term here represents a loss.

commonMistakes: Matching the larger number to the larger-sounding quantity instead of testing r = 0.
tips: In an expression of the form (rate)(variable) + (constant), the constant is always the value when the variable is zero.

whyCorrect: Solve the inequality: subtract 8 from both sides to get \(5x\le 35\) , then divide by 5 to get \(x\le 7\) . The greatest whole number of strings that satisfies it is 7, and 5(7) + 8 = 43 exactly meets the limit.

whyWrong.A: 5 is safe but not the greatest: 5(5) + 8 = 33, well under 43.
whyWrong.C: 9 gives 5(9) + 8 = 53, which exceeds 43.
whyWrong.D: 35 is the value of 5x after subtracting 8; it still has to be divided by 5.

commonMistakes: Stopping at 5x ≤ 35 and reporting 35.
tips: Substitute your answer back into the original inequality — it should come out true, and one more should come out false.

whyCorrect: Substitute f = 22 into 7f + 40. Multiply first: 7(22) = 154, then add the fixed 40 to get 194 pence.

whyWrong.A: 154 is 7(22) with the 40-pence fixed charge left off.
whyWrong.B: 180 is 7(20) + 40, using 20 fish instead of 22.
whyWrong.D: 234 adds the 40 twice.

commonMistakes: Adding the 40 to the 22 before multiplying by 7.
tips: Order of operations: the multiplication attached to the variable happens before the constant is added.

whyCorrect: Look for the greatest number that divides both 15 and 35. That is 5, since 15 = 5(3) and 35 = 5(7), so \(15p+35=5(3p+7)\) . Distributing back confirms it: 5(3p) = 15p and 5(7) = 35.

whyWrong.A: \(3(5p+7)\) expands to 15p + 21, not 15p + 35.
whyWrong.C: \(5(3p+35)\) expands to 15p + 175 — the 35 was not divided by the 5 taken out.

commonMistakes: Factoring out a number from the first term only and leaving the constant untouched.
tips: Always expand your factored form back out; it takes a few seconds and catches every error of this kind.

whyCorrect: A square root applies to each factor: \(\sqrt{81}=9\) and \(\sqrt{b^{4}}=b^{2}\) , because \(\left(b^{2}\right)^{2}=b^{4}\) . So the figure is \(9b^{2}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(9b^{4}\) takes the root of 81 but leaves the exponent on b unchanged; taking a square root halves the exponent.
whyWrong.C: \(18b^{2}\) halves 81's coefficient in the wrong way — 18 is 2(9), not \(\sqrt{81}\) .
whyWrong.D: \(81b^{2}\) handles the variable correctly but never takes the square root of 81.

commonMistakes: Halving the coefficient instead of taking its square root.
tips: Test b = 1: the expression is \(\sqrt{81}=9\) , so any choice that does not give 9 at b = 1 is out.

whyCorrect: Substitute x = 8 into \(\frac{120}{x}\) , which gives \(\frac{120}{8}=15\) days.

whyWrong.A: 8 is the value of x itself, not the result of the division.
whyWrong.B: 10 is 120/12, using the wrong divisor.
whyWrong.C: 12 is 120/10; it also comes from reading the 120 as 12.

commonMistakes: Multiplying 120 by 8 instead of dividing.
tips: A warmer cave (larger x) should mean fewer days, and 15 is less than the 120 days the model gives at x = 1, which fits.

whyWrong.A: 3 gives \(5^{3}=125\) , one factor of 5 short.
whyWrong.C: 5 gives \(5^{5}=3125\) , far too large.
whyWrong.D: 125 is \(5^{3}\) , a value of the expression rather than a value of the exponent.

commonMistakes: Dividing 625 by 5 and answering with the result instead of counting how many times you divided.
tips: Keep multiplying the base until you reach the target and count the factors — that count is the exponent.

whyCorrect: Work the denominator first: at x = 7 it is 7 + 3 = 10. Then \(\frac{200}{10}=20\) minutes.
commonMistakes: Dividing 200 by 7 and then adding 3, which ignores that the whole denominator is x + 3.
tips: A fraction bar groups everything under it, so finish the bottom before dividing.

whyCorrect: Take out the common factor 4 first: \(4y^{2}-36=4\left(y^{2}-9\right)\) . What is left is a difference of two squares, since \(9=3^{2}\) , so \(y^{2}-9=(y-3)(y+3)\) . The full factorisation is \(4(y-3)(y+3)\) .

whyWrong.A: \(4(y-3)^{2}\) expands to \(4y^{2}-24y+36\) , which has a y term the original does not.
whyWrong.C: \(4(y-6)(y+6)\) expands to \(4y^{2}-144\) — it uses 6 as the square root of 36 without first removing the factor 4.

commonMistakes: Taking the square root of 36 as 6 while leaving the 4 in front, which double-counts the factor of 4.
tips: Pull out the common numerical factor before you look for a difference of squares.

whyCorrect: Compare the four counts by their leading digits: 2,140 and 2,905 both start with 2 thousand, while 3,480 and 3,260 are in the 3 thousands. Between those two, 3,480 is greater than 3,260, so Garrow smoked the most.

whyWrong.A: Fennhaven's 2,140 is the smallest of the four.
whyWrong.C: Halden smoked 2,905, still short of 3,000.
whyWrong.D: Ivory Quay's 3,260 is second: it beats both 2-thousand figures but is 220 short of Garrow.

commonMistakes: Comparing only the last digits, or reading 3,260 as larger than 3,480 because 6 is larger than 4.
tips: With four-digit figures, compare digits left to right and stop at the first place where they differ.

whyCorrect: Percent means the part over the whole, times 100. The part is 12 and the whole is all 60 wheels, so \(\frac{12}{60}=0.2\) , which is 20 percent.

whyWrong.A: 12% repeats the count of wrapped wheels as though it were already a percentage.
whyWrong.B: 15% would need 9 wrapped wheels out of 60.
whyWrong.D: 25% comes from dividing 12 by the 48 bare wheels instead of by all 60.

commonMistakes: Using the leftover group as the denominator; the whole includes the part you are measuring.
tips: Check it back: 20 percent of 60 is 12.

whyCorrect: A steady rate times the time gives the total: 2.5(14). Since 2.5 is two and a half, that is 2(14) + 0.5(14) = 28 + 7 = 35 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 16.5 adds 14 and 2.5 instead of multiplying.
whyWrong.B: 28 is 2(14), dropping the half-kilogram part of the rate.
whyWrong.D: 56 is 4(14), which doubles the rate rather than using 2.5.

commonMistakes: Rounding 2.5 to 2 or 3 before multiplying.
tips: Split an awkward decimal rate into whole and fractional parts and multiply each one.

whyCorrect: The whole is every wheel graded, so add all three grades: 36 + 27 + 17 = 80. The prime fraction is \(\frac{36}{80}\) , and dividing top and bottom by 4 gives \(\frac{9}{20}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{9}{25}\) is \(\frac{36}{100}\) , using 100 as the total instead of the 80 wheels actually graded.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{4}{9}\) comes from dividing 36 by a total that leaves out the kitchen grade or miscounts it.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{27}{80}\) has the right total but uses the second grade's 27 wheels in the numerator.

commonMistakes: Assuming the total is a round number like 100 rather than adding the rows.
tips: Add the table's rows first and write the total down; every part-to-whole question in the set then uses it.

whyCorrect: Add the four shelf counts: 46 + 38 = 84, 84 + 52 = 136, and 136 + 29 = 165 wheels.

whyWrong.A: 148 falls short by 17, typically from dropping part of one shelf's count while carrying.
whyWrong.B: 155 misses by 10, a carrying slip in the tens column.
whyWrong.D: 173 overshoots by 8.

commonMistakes: Adding all four numbers in one pass without writing down the running total.
tips: Pair the numbers into easy sums: 46 + 29 = 75 and 38 + 52 = 90, and 75 + 90 = 165.

whyCorrect: Start with the full rectangle: 120(45) = 5,400 square centimetres. The square cut out has area 15(15) = 225 square centimetres, and it is removed, so the board is 5400 - 225 = 5,175 square centimetres.

whyWrong.B: 5,220 subtracts 180 rather than 225, using 15(12) or the square's perimeter instead of its area.
whyWrong.C: 5,400 is the rectangle before the corner is cut out.
whyWrong.D: 5,625 adds the 225 instead of subtracting it.

commonMistakes: Using the side of the cut-out square, 15, as the amount to remove instead of its area.
tips: Whenever a shape has a piece removed, compute both areas separately and subtract at the end.

whyCorrect: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so 3n + 4n + 5n = 180. That is 12n = 180, giving n = 15. The angles are then 45, 60 and 75 degrees, which do add to 180.

whyWrong.A: 12 is the coefficient 3 + 4 + 5, not the value of n.
whyWrong.C: 18 comes from dividing 180 by 10 and adjusting, and it gives angles of 54, 72 and 90 degrees totalling 216.
whyWrong.D: 20 divides 180 by 9 rather than by 12, giving angles that total 240 degrees.

commonMistakes: Using 360 degrees, which is the angle sum for a quadrilateral, not a triangle.
tips: Substitute your n back and check the three angles really add to 180.

whyCorrect: A prism's volume is the area of its cross-section times its height. The square cross-section has area 0.9(0.9) = 0.81 square metre, so the inside volume is 0.81(7) = 5.67 cubic metres.
commonMistakes: Multiplying 0.9 by 7 and stopping, which uses only one side of the square.
tips: Square the side before multiplying by the height, and keep both decimal places: \(0.9^{2}=0.81\) , not 8.1.

whyCorrect: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is the longest side, so the two equal sides must be the legs. With legs of 9, the third side is \(\sqrt{9^{2}+9^{2}}=\sqrt{162}=9\sqrt{2}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(9\sqrt{3}\) belongs to a 30-60-90 triangle, not to a right triangle with two equal legs.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}\) is the leg you would get if 9 were the hypotenuse; here 9 is a leg, so the answer must be longer than 9.
whyWrong.D: 18 doubles a leg instead of using the Pythagorean theorem; two sides of 9 cannot meet a third side of 18 at all.

commonMistakes: Adding the legs, which always overshoots — the hypotenuse is about 12.7, not 18.
tips: A right isosceles triangle is always in the ratio \(1:1:\sqrt{2}\) .

whyCorrect: Use the equation without the unknown constant first. Putting x = 3 into 3x - 2y = 5 gives 9 - 2y = 5, so 2y = 4 and y = 2. Now substitute both values into the other equation: a(3) + 4(2) = 26, so 3a = 18 and a = 6.

whyWrong.A: 2 is the value of y, found on the way but not what the question asks for.
whyWrong.B: 4 is the coefficient of y in the first equation, not the constant a.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the number on the right of the second equation.

commonMistakes: Trying to solve the system with a still in it; the second equation alone pins down y once x is known.
tips: Check the finished equation: 6(3) + 4(2) = 18 + 8 = 26.

whyCorrect: There are n batches, each spending t hours in the smoke, giving nt hours of smoking. Cooling happens only between batches, so with n batches there are n - 1 gaps, not n — the clock stops when the last batch comes out, before any further cooling. Total time is \(nt+(n-1)c\) .

whyWrong.B: nt + nc counts a cooling period after the final batch, which happens after the moment the question stops timing.
whyWrong.C: \((n-1)t+nc\) puts the n - 1 on the wrong quantity: every batch is smoked, but only the gaps between them are counted.
whyWrong.D: \(n(t+c)-t\) expands to nt + nc - t; it removes one smoking period instead of one cooling period, so it is right only in the special case t = c.

commonMistakes: Counting one gap per batch rather than one gap per pair of consecutive batches.
tips: Test n = 2: one batch smokes, the hearth cools once, the second batch smokes, so the total is 2t + c.

whyCorrect: Let L and S be the two ovens' counts, so L + S = 348. After moving 40 fish the larger holds L - 40 and the smaller holds S + 40, and the condition is L - 40 = (S + 40) + 26. That simplifies to L - S = 106. Adding L + S = 348 gives 2L = 454, so L = 227 (and S = 121).
commonMistakes: Writing L - 40 = S + 26 and forgetting that the 40 fish arrive in the smaller oven as well as leaving the larger one.
tips: Check the described situation: 187 and 161 differ by 26, and 187 + 161 = 348.

whyCorrect: The slope is \(\frac{11a-3a}{3a-a}=\frac{8a}{2a}=4\) , so a cancels and the slope is 4. Using the point \((a,3a)\) , the equation is y = 4x + b with 3a = 4a + b, so b = -a.

whyWrong.B: a has the right size but the wrong sign: 4a is larger than 3a, so the intercept must be negative.
whyWrong.C: -4a multiplies the slope by a instead of subtracting 4a from 3a.
whyWrong.D: 3a is the y-coordinate of the given point \((a,3a)\) , which is not on the vertical axis.

commonMistakes: Assuming the line passes through the origin because both given points have y a multiple of x.
tips: Check the finished line y = 4x - a against the second point: 4(3a) - a = 11a.

whyCorrect: An absolute value at most 2.5 means the distance from m to 38 is at most 2.5 in either direction, so \(-2.5\le m-38\le 2.5\) . Adding 38 throughout gives \(35.5\le m\le 40.5\) .

whyWrong.B: \(35.5\le m\le 38\) keeps only the masses below 38; a wheel of 39 kilograms is 1 kilogram from 38 and is acceptable.
whyWrong.C: \(m\le 35.5\) or \(m\ge 40.5\) is the solution of the opposite condition, \(\left|m-38\right|\ge 2.5\) .
whyWrong.D: \(38\le m\le 40.5\) keeps only the masses above 38.

commonMistakes: Treating the absolute value as if it only allowed the positive side of 38.
tips: Read \(\left|m-38\right|\le 2.5\) as "m is within 2.5 of 38" and write the centre plus and minus the tolerance.

whyCorrect: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so p is the slope through the two given points: \(\frac{17-5}{4-1}=\frac{12}{3}=4\) . The line passes through \((0,-5)\) , so q, the y-intercept, is -5. Then p + q = 4 + (-5) = -1.

whyWrong.A: -9 subtracts the slope from the intercept, -5 - 4, instead of adding them.
whyWrong.C: 3 uses a slope of 8 or the run 3 in place of the slope of 4.
whyWrong.D: 9 adds 4 and 5 while dropping the minus sign on the intercept.

commonMistakes: Reading \((0,-5)\) as giving a positive intercept, or computing the slope as \(\frac{4-1}{17-5}\) .
tips: The y-intercept is handed to you whenever a point has x = 0 — no substitution needed.

whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by 4, which is positive so the inequality keeps its direction: \(5x-3\ge 4(x+2)\) , that is \(5x-3\ge 4x+8\) . Subtracting 4x and adding 3 gives \(x\ge 11\) .

whyWrong.B: \(x\le 11\) reverses the inequality; you only flip the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number, and 4 is positive.
whyWrong.C: \(x\ge\frac{5}{4}\) fails a quick test: at x = 2 the left side is \(\frac{7}{4}\) and the right side is 4, so the condition does not hold.
whyWrong.D: \(x\le -\frac{11}{9}\) comes from adding 4x to both sides instead of subtracting it, giving 9x, and then flipping the sign as well.

commonMistakes: Multiplying only the numerator on the left by 4 and leaving the right side alone.
tips: Check the boundary: at x = 11 both sides equal 13, so 11 itself is included.

whyCorrect: \(g(x)=f(x+2)\) is zero exactly when the input to f is a zero of f, so set x + 2 = -4 and x + 2 = 6. Those give x = -6 and x = 4, which is the graph of f shifted 2 to the left. The greater of the two is 4.

whyWrong.A: -6 is the lesser of g's two zeros.
whyWrong.B: -2 is -4 + 2, shifting the wrong way and using the wrong zero.
whyWrong.D: 8 is 6 + 2, shifting right; replacing x by x + 2 moves the graph left, because the input reaches each value 2 units sooner.

commonMistakes: Assuming "+2" inside the function moves the graph in the positive x direction.
tips: Decide the shift by solving the inside for zero rather than memorising a direction: x + 2 = 6 gives x = 4.

whyCorrect: Complete the square: half of 14 is 7, and \((x+7)^{2}=x^{2}+14x+49\) . The original constant is 58, which is 9 more than 49, so \(x^{2}+14x+58=(x+7)^{2}+9\) .

whyWrong.B: \((x+7)^{2}-9\) expands to \(x^{2}+14x+40\) ; the 49 must be made up to 58, not cut down.
whyWrong.C: \((x+7)^{2}+58\) adds the original constant again on top of the 49 already inside the square.
whyWrong.D: \((x+14)^{2}-138\) halves nothing: it uses 14 inside the bracket, which produces a middle term of 28x.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that squaring (x + 7) already contributes 49 to the constant.
tips: Check at x = 0: the original gives 58, and \(49+9=58\) .

whyCorrect: For the expression to be a perfect square it must be \((2x+7)^{2}\) , since \(\sqrt{4x^{2}}=2x\) and \(\sqrt{49}=7\) . Expanding gives \(4x^{2}+28x+49\) , so k = 28. The middle term is twice the product of the two roots: 2(2)(7) = 28.

whyWrong.A: 14 is 2(7), which would be the middle coefficient if the leading term were \(x^{2}\) rather than \(4x^{2}\) .
whyWrong.B: 21 is 3(7) and matches no expansion here.
whyWrong.C: 26 is close to 28 but makes the expression fail to factor: \(4x^{2}+26x+49\) has discriminant 676 - 784, which is negative.

commonMistakes: Taking the middle coefficient as the product of the two constants, 2(7) = 14, instead of twice that product.
tips: For \((ax+b)^{2}\) the middle coefficient is always 2ab.

whyCorrect: Write 9 as \(3^{2}\) , so \(9^{\frac{t}{2}}=\left(3^{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{2}}\) . A power of a power multiplies the exponents: \(2\cdot\frac{t}{2}=t\) . So \(R(t)=6\cdot 3^{t}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(6\cdot 3^{2t}\) multiplies where it should divide: \(2\cdot\frac{t}{2}\) is t, not 2t.
whyWrong.C: \(18^{\frac{t}{2}}\) folds the coefficient 6 into the base, but the 6 multiplies the power rather than being raised to it.
whyWrong.D: \(6\cdot 81^{t}\) squares the base a second time, giving \(3^{4t}\) .

commonMistakes: Multiplying the coefficient into the base when a number sits in front of an exponential.
tips: Test t = 2: the model gives 6(9) = 54, and \(6\cdot 3^{2}=54\) as well.

whyCorrect: Square the expression you want: \(\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{2}=x^{2}+2\left(x\right)\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) , and the middle term is just 2 because the x cancels. So the square equals 23 + 2 = 25, and since x is positive the value is 5.
commonMistakes: Trying to solve \(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}=23\) for x itself; squaring the requested expression is far quicker and avoids radicals entirely.
tips: Whenever a question gives \(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) and asks for \(x+\frac{1}{x}\) , the link is always the cross term 2.

whyCorrect: Set the model to zero: \(-3x^{2}+42x-135=0\) . Divide through by -3 to get \(x^{2}-14x+45=0\) , which factors as (x - 5)(x - 9) = 0. The two values are 5 and 9, and their positive difference is 4.

whyWrong.A: 2 is half the difference, the distance from either root to the vertex at x = 7.
whyWrong.B: 3 would come from roots such as 5 and 8, which do not satisfy the equation.
whyWrong.D: 9 is one of the two roots, not the gap between them.

commonMistakes: Trying to factor with the -3 still in front instead of dividing it out first.
tips: Check the factorisation by expanding: (x - 5)(x - 9) gives \(x^{2}-14x+45\) .

whyCorrect: Work in totals. The first 45 wheels weigh 45(4.2) = 189 kilograms, and the new wheels add 6w. The new mean is \(\frac{189+6w}{45+w}=4.5\) , so 189 + 6w = 4.5(45 + w) = 202.5 + 4.5w. That gives 1.5w = 13.5 and w = 9.

whyWrong.A: 6 gives a mean of \(\frac{189+36}{51}\) , about 4.41 kilograms — not far enough.
whyWrong.C: 12 gives \(\frac{189+72}{57}\) , about 4.58 kilograms — past 4.5.
whyWrong.D: 15 gives \(\frac{189+90}{60}\) , about 4.65 kilograms.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the denominator grows too: adding wheels changes both the total mass and the count.
tips: Each new wheel is 1.5 kilograms above the old mean and has to lift 45 wheels by 0.3 each, so w(1.5) = 45(0.3).

whyCorrect: Direct variation means the hourly output per rack is constant: 45/3 = 15 fish an hour per rack. With 5 racks the smokehouse cures 5(15) = 75 fish an hour, so 1,200 fish take 1200/75 = 16 hours.

whyWrong.A: 12 corresponds to a rate of 100 fish an hour, which no number of racks here produces.
whyWrong.C: 20 uses 60 fish an hour, which adds one rack's worth to the 45 rather than scaling to 5 racks.
whyWrong.D: 27 uses the original 45 fish an hour, ignoring the extra racks entirely.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the time by 5/3 instead of dividing; more racks means fewer hours.
tips: Find the per-unit rate first, then scale it — it keeps the direction of the change obvious.

whyCorrect: "4.0 kilograms or more" covers the last two rows, 31 + 14 = 45 wheels. As a share of all 80, that is \(\frac{45}{80}=0.5625\) , or 56.25 percent.

whyWrong.A: 17.5% is only the 4.5-to-4.9 class, 14 wheels out of 80.
whyWrong.B: 38.75% is only the 4.0-to-4.4 class, 31 wheels out of 80.
whyWrong.C: 43.75% is the 35 wheels below 4.0 kilograms — the complement of the group asked for.

commonMistakes: Counting only the row that starts at 4.0 and forgetting that every heavier class also qualifies.
tips: Check that your percent and its complement add to 100: 56.25 + 43.75 = 100.

whyCorrect: The wheel is selected from the upper cave only, so the denominator is that row's total of 120, not 240. Of those 120 wheels, 84 were graded prime, so the probability is \(\frac{84}{120}=\frac{7}{10}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{7}{20}\) is \(\frac{84}{240}\) , dividing by every wheel in both caves.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{43}{80}\) is \(\frac{129}{240}\) , the share of all wheels that are prime, which ignores the upper-cave restriction.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{28}{43}\) is \(\frac{84}{129}\) , which conditions on the prime column instead: the chance a prime wheel came from the upper cave.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the grand total whenever a two-way table gives one.
tips: The phrase "selected from the wheels in the upper cave" fixes the denominator before you look at anything else.

whyCorrect: Write the original counts as 5x Tomme and 3x Beaufort. After the delivery the Beaufort count is 3x + 48, and \(\frac{5x}{3x+48}=\frac{5}{4}\) . Cross-multiplying gives 20x = 15x + 240, so 5x = 240 — and 5x is exactly the number of Tomme wheels, 240.

whyWrong.A: 144 is the original number of Beaufort wheels, 3x with x = 48.
whyWrong.B: 180 fails the check: with 180 Tomme the cave would hold 108 Beaufort, and 108 + 48 = 156 gives a ratio of 15 to 13.
whyWrong.C: 192 is the Beaufort count after the 48 arrive, not the Tomme count.

commonMistakes: Solving for x and reporting it instead of the quantity 5x that the question asks about.
tips: Check both ratios at the end: 240 to 144 reduces to 5 to 3, and 240 to 192 reduces to 5 to 4.

whyCorrect: With no base, the metal is the cone's lateral surface, \(\pi rl\) , where l is the slant length running along the sheet. Here r = 60 and l = 100, so the area is \(\pi(60)(100)=6{,}000\pi\) square centimetres.

whyWrong.A: \(1{,}200\pi\) is five times too small; it pairs the radius with 20 rather than with the 100-centimetre slant.
whyWrong.B: \(3{,}000\pi\) halves the lateral area, borrowing the \(\frac{1}{2}\) from the area of a triangle.
whyWrong.C: \(4{,}800\pi\) uses the vertical height 80 (from the 60-80-100 right triangle) in place of the slant length; lateral area needs the slant.

commonMistakes: Adding \(\pi r^{2}\) for a base that the question says is not there.
tips: The 60, 80, 100 triple is there to tempt you into the height; \(\pi rl\) always takes the slant.

whyCorrect: The first triangle has a right angle at \((12,0)\) with legs 12 and 5, so its hypotenuse is 13 and its area is \(\frac{1}{2}(12)(5)=30\) . The second triangle's longest side is 39, so the scale factor is 39/13 = 3. Areas scale by the square of the factor, so the area is \(30(3^{2})=270\) square centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 90 multiplies the area by 3 instead of by \(3^{2}\) .
whyWrong.B: 180 uses a factor of 6 on the area rather than 9.
whyWrong.D: 390 is 39(10), mixing a side length with an area.

commonMistakes: Scaling area by the same factor as length; doubling every length quadruples the area.
tips: Find the scale factor from corresponding sides first, then square it for areas and cube it for volumes.

whyCorrect: The room's full volume is 12(7)(3) = 252 cubic metres. Each pier runs the full 3-metre height with a cross-section of 0.5(0.5) = 0.25 square metre, so each takes up 0.25(3) = 0.75 cubic metre, and four of them take 3 cubic metres. The space left is 252 - 3 = 249 cubic metres.
commonMistakes: Subtracting only one pier, or using 0.5 as the cross-sectional area instead of 0.25.
tips: Compute one pier's volume completely, then multiply by the number of piers before subtracting.

whyCorrect: The right angle is at C, so AB is the hypotenuse and \(\cos A=\frac{AC}{AB}=\frac{20}{29}\) . Since AB = 87 = 3(29), the triangle is a 20-21-29 right triangle scaled by 3: AC = 60 and BC = 63 (check: \(87^{2}-60^{2}=3969=63^{2}\) ). The perimeter is 60 + 63 + 87 = 210 centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 147 is 60 + 87, leaving out the third side BC.
whyWrong.B: 183 is 60 + 63 + 60, using the leg AC a second time in place of the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: 234 is 60 + 87 + 87, counting the hypotenuse twice.

commonMistakes: Treating 87 as a leg; the side opposite the right angle is always the hypotenuse, and \(\cos A\) compares the adjacent leg to it.
tips: Recognising \(\frac{20}{29}\) as part of the 20-21-29 triple saves the Pythagorean arithmetic.

whyCorrect: Let T be the takings. Two fifths go to the proprietor, so three fifths remain; then £7 goes for stabling and £53 is left. That gives \(\frac{3}{5}T-7=53\) , so \(\frac{3}{5}T=60\) and T = £100.

whyWrong.B: £110 leaves \(\frac{3}{5}(110)=66\) after the proprietor and £59 after stabling, not £53.
whyWrong.C: £120 leaves £72 and then £65.
whyWrong.D: £150 leaves £90 and then £83.

commonMistakes: Adding the £7 back after undoing the fraction rather than before; the stabling comes out of what was already left.
tips: Undo the steps in reverse order: add the 7 first to reach 60, and only then divide by 3/5.

whyCorrect: Going from 4 passengers to 9 adds 5 passengers and 1861 - 1486 = 375 kilograms, so each passenger with luggage weighs 375/5 = 75 kilograms. The empty coach is then 1486 - 4(75) = 1486 - 300 = 1,186 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 811 subtracts 9 passengers' worth (675 kilograms) from the 4-passenger weight.
whyWrong.B: 1,036 subtracts 450 kilograms, six passengers' worth.
whyWrong.C: 1,111 subtracts the whole 375-kilogram difference, which is five passengers, not the four actually aboard.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the difference in weights directly instead of first finding the weight of one passenger.
tips: Check with the other reading: 1186 + 9(75) = 1,861 kilograms.

whyCorrect: An average of at least 15 over six journeys needs a total of at least 6(15) = 90 parcels. The first five journeys give 12 + 18 + 9 + 16 + 14 = 69, so the sixth must supply at least 90 - 69 = 21.

whyWrong.A: 19 brings the total to 88, an average of about 14.7.
whyWrong.B: 20 brings the total to 89, still short of 90.
whyWrong.D: 22 does meet the requirement but is one more than necessary; the question asks for the least.

commonMistakes: Averaging the five journeys and comparing that with 15, which does not tell you what the sixth must be.
tips: Turn an average requirement into a total requirement first; it converts the problem into simple addition.

whyCorrect: After the head office sells three eighths, five eighths of the places are still unsold. Those remaining places are the 20 sold at wayside offices plus the 5 never sold, so \(\frac{5}{8}N=25\) and N = 40. Checking: 15 go at the head office, 25 remain, and 20 + 5 accounts for them.

whyWrong.B: 45 leaves \(\frac{5}{8}(45)\) , which is not even a whole number of places.
whyWrong.C: 56 leaves 35 places after the head office, ten more than the 25 accounted for.
whyWrong.D: 64 leaves 40 places after the head office, not 25.

commonMistakes: Applying the 20 and 5 to the whole coach rather than to the places still unsold.
tips: When a fraction is taken "of what remains", name the remainder as its own quantity before setting up the equation.

whyCorrect: Write the three stables as 2x, 3x and 5x. The largest exceeds the smallest by 5x - 2x = 3x, and that equals 18, so x = 6. The stables hold 12, 18 and 30 horses, a total of 10x = 60.

whyWrong.A: 45 would make the parts 9, 13.5 and 22.5 — not whole horses, and the largest exceeds the smallest by 13.5.
whyWrong.C: 72 makes the largest exceed the smallest by 21.6, not 18.
whyWrong.D: 90 comes from comparing the largest stable with the middle one (5x - 3x = 2x = 18), which is not what the question says.

commonMistakes: Setting the ratio difference against the wrong pair of stables.
tips: Check the finished numbers against every stated condition: 30 - 12 = 18, and 12 : 18 : 30 reduces to 2 : 3 : 5.

whyCorrect: Set the two prices equal: 54 + 3L = 30 + 5L. Subtract 3L and 30 from both sides to get 24 = 2L, so L = 12 lights. At 12 lights both charge £90.

whyWrong.A: 6 lights cost £72 from Alder and £60 from Birch.
whyWrong.B: 8 divides the £24 gap by 3 (one builder's rate) instead of by the £2 difference in rates.
whyWrong.C: 10 lights cost £84 from Alder and £80 from Birch — closer, but still not equal.

commonMistakes: Dividing the difference in fixed sums by one rate rather than by the difference between the rates.
tips: Birch starts £24 cheaper and gains £2 a light, so it takes 24/2 = 12 lights to catch up.

whyCorrect: Let I be the inside places, so the outside places number 51 - I. The receipts give 8I + 5(51 - I) = 333, that is 3I + 255 = 333. So 3I = 78 and I = 26 inside places (with 25 outside).
commonMistakes: Dividing 333 by 8 or by 13 instead of setting up the two conditions together.
tips: Check both: 26 + 25 = 51 places, and 8(26) + 5(25) = 208 + 125 = 333 shillings.

whyCorrect: Vertex form shows the best fare as the number subtracted inside the bracket. Factor -2 from the first two terms: \(-2\left(f^{2}-18f\right)+40\) . Completing the square inside needs \((f-9)^{2}-81\) , and multiplying that -81 by -2 adds 162, giving \(-2(f-9)^{2}+202\) . The fare of 9 shillings gives the greatest takings, £202.

whyWrong.B: \(-2(f-9)^{2}+121\) has the right bracket but the wrong constant; it expands to \(-2f^{2}+36f-41\) .
whyWrong.C: \(-2(f+9)^{2}+202\) puts the maximum at f = -9, a negative fare, and expands with -36f.
whyWrong.D: \(-2(f-18)^{2}+364\) uses 18 rather than half of 18 inside the bracket, producing a middle term of 72f.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the -81 inside the bracket is multiplied by the -2 outside before it reaches the constant.
tips: Check at f = 0: the original gives 40, and \(-2(81)+202=40\) .

whyCorrect: Set the model equal to 33 and clear the fraction: \(\frac{18n+540}{n}=33\) gives 18n + 540 = 33n. Then 540 = 15n, so n = 36 coaches.

whyWrong.A: 30 coaches give an average of (540 + 540)/30 = £36 each.
whyWrong.C: 45 coaches give (810 + 540)/45 = £30 each.
whyWrong.D: 60 coaches give (1080 + 540)/60 = £27 each.

commonMistakes: Splitting the fraction as 18n + 540/n and then dropping the n from the first term.
tips: The model is really 18 + 540/n, so you need 540/n = 15.

whyCorrect: For \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) the two solutions add to \(-\frac{b}{a}\) , which here is \(\frac{11}{2}\) . One solution is 4, so the other is \(\frac{11}{2}-4=\frac{3}{2}\) . Checking with k = 12: \(2(16)-11(4)+12=0\) and \(2\left(\frac{9}{4}\right)-11\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)+12=0\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{4}{3}\) comes from treating the leading 2 as if it divided the 4 rather than the 11.
whyWrong.D: 3 would make the solutions add to 7, which is \(-\frac{b}{a}\) only if the leading coefficient were 1 and b were -7.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the leading coefficient 2 and taking the sum of the solutions to be 11.
tips: With one root given and k unknown, the sum of the roots is the only relation you need — the product involves k.

whyCorrect: Every term has a factor of 2x, so start there: \(4x^{3}+6x^{2}-10x=2x\left(2x^{2}+3x-5\right)\) . The quadratic factors because 2(-5) = -10 splits as 5 and -2, which add to 3: \(2x^{2}+5x-2x-5=(2x+5)(x-1)\) . So the allowance is \(2x(2x+5)(x-1)\) .

whyWrong.B: \(2x(2x-5)(x+1)\) multiplies out to \(2x\left(2x^{2}-3x-5\right)\) , with the middle sign reversed.

commonMistakes: Pairing the 5 with the wrong bracket, which changes the middle coefficient from 3 to 9.
tips: Multiply any candidate back out and compare middle terms — that alone separates all four choices here.

whyCorrect: Inverse variation means the product of the two quantities is constant. Here 24(15) = 360 horse-days of oats in the stock, and that total does not change. With 40 horses eating it, 360/40 = 9 days.

whyWrong.A: 8 days would feed 40 horses for only 320 horse-days, less than the stock holds.
whyWrong.C: 12 days would need 480 horse-days, more than the stock holds.
whyWrong.D: 25 scales the days up in step with the horses, which is direct variation; more horses must mean fewer days.

commonMistakes: Setting up the proportion 24/15 = 40/d, which treats the relationship as direct.
tips: For inverse variation write \(d_{1}h_{1}=d_{2}h_{2}\) and check the direction: the answer must be less than 15.

whyCorrect: If the yard japans x lamps a day, it takes \(\frac{60}{x}\) days; at x + 5 a day it would take \(\frac{60}{x+5}\) days, one day fewer. So \(\frac{60}{x}-\frac{60}{x+5}=1\) . Multiplying through by x(x + 5) gives 60(x + 5) - 60x = x(x + 5), that is 300 = \(x^{2}+5x\) . Then \(x^{2}+5x-300=0\) factors as (x + 20)(x - 15) = 0, and only x = 15 makes sense.
commonMistakes: Writing the equation the other way round, \(\frac{60}{x+5}-\frac{60}{x}=1\) , which gives a negative rate; the faster pace takes fewer days, so it is the smaller time.
tips: Check it: 60/15 = 4 days, and 60/20 = 3 days, exactly one day sooner.

whyCorrect: Divide taken-up places by booked places at each office: Ashby 186/240 = 77.5 percent, Bramber 144/180 = 80 percent, Corve 231/300 = 77 percent, Denby 117/150 = 78 percent. Bramber has the greatest share.

whyWrong.A: Ashby's 186 out of 240 is 77.5 percent, below Bramber's 80.
whyWrong.C: Corve booked and took up the most places in raw numbers but has the lowest rate, 77 percent.
whyWrong.D: Denby's 117 out of 150 is 78 percent.

commonMistakes: Comparing the numbers of places taken up rather than the proportion of each office's own bookings.
tips: Convert each row to a decimal before comparing — the largest office is not the one with the best rate here.

whyCorrect: There are 28 brass lamps and 63 - 28 = 35 japanned ones. Three quarters of the brass is 21 repaired, and two fifths of the japanned is 14 repaired, giving 35 repaired lamps in all. The probability is \(\frac{35}{63}=\frac{5}{9}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{3}\) is \(\frac{21}{63}\) , counting only the repaired brass lamps.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{4}{9}\) is \(\frac{28}{63}\) , the share of lamps that are brass rather than repaired.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{2}\) comes from averaging the two fractions \(\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{2}{5}\) instead of applying each to its own group.

commonMistakes: Averaging two rates when the two groups are different sizes.
tips: Turn each fraction into a count of lamps first, add the counts, and only then divide by 63.

whyCorrect: Convert to the units the coverage is quoted in: 288 square feet divided by 9 square feet per square yard is 32 square yards. At 4 square yards a pint, that needs 32/4 = 8 pints.

whyWrong.A: 2 pints cover 8 square yards, which is 72 square feet.
whyWrong.B: 4 pints cover 16 square yards, or 144 square feet — half the panelling.
whyWrong.C: 6 pints cover 24 square yards, or 216 square feet.

commonMistakes: Dividing 288 by 4 while the figure is still in square feet, which mixes the two units.
tips: Make the units match before dividing, and check backwards: 8 pints cover 32 square yards, which is 288 square feet.

whyCorrect: Add all four builds for the total: 24 + 15 + 36 + 45 = 120 carriages. Landaus and barouches together are 36 + 15 = 51, so the probability is \(\frac{51}{120}\) , which reduces by 3 to \(\frac{17}{40}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{8}\) is \(\frac{45}{120}\) , the broughams.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{7}{24}\) matches no group here; the two builds asked about come to 51 of 120.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{17}{23}\) is \(\frac{51}{69}\) , dividing by the 69 other carriages instead of by all 120.

commonMistakes: Adding the two probabilities as fractions with different denominators instead of adding the counts first.
tips: For an "or" question about separate categories, add the counts, then divide once.

whyCorrect: Set up the proportion \(\frac{3}{7}=\frac{6.75}{L}\) . Since 6.75 is 2.25 times 3, the real length is 2.25 times 7, which is 15.75 feet.

whyWrong.A: 14 is 2(7), which uses 6 inches on the drawing rather than 6.75.
whyWrong.C: 16.5 fails the proportion: 6.75/16.5 is about 0.409, not 3/7 = 0.4286.
whyWrong.D: 18 scales by \(\frac{8}{3}\) instead of \(\frac{7}{3}\) .

commonMistakes: Multiplying 6.75 by 3 and dividing by 7, which inverts the scale.
tips: Ask which quantity should be larger: the carriage is real and the drawing is small, so the answer must exceed 6.75 by the factor 7/3.

whyCorrect: An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles, so the three angles are 4x, x + 30 and x + 30, and they add to 180. That gives 4x + 2x + 60 = 180, so 6x = 120 and x = 20. The angle between the equal sides is 4x = 80 degrees.

whyWrong.A: 50 is x + 30, one of the base angles.
whyWrong.B: 60 would need x = 15, and then the three angles would total only 150 degrees.
whyWrong.D: 100 is 180 - 80, the supplement of the apex angle rather than the angle itself.

commonMistakes: Counting the base angle once instead of twice when writing the angle sum.
tips: Check the finished triangle: 80 + 50 + 50 = 180.

whyCorrect: A trapezium's area is the average of the parallel sides times the distance between them: \(\frac{58+74}{2}(40)=66(40)=2{,}640\) square inches for one face. Each panel has two faces painted, and there are two panels, so four faces in all: 2640(4) = 10,560 square inches.

whyWrong.A: 2,640 is one face of one panel.
whyWrong.B: 5,280 counts two faces — either both faces of one panel or one face of each — but there are four.
whyWrong.D: 21,120 counts eight faces, doubling one step too many.

commonMistakes: Adding the parallel sides without halving, or forgetting that "both faces of each panel" doubles a quantity that is already doubled by there being two panels.
tips: Count the painted surfaces explicitly: 2 panels times 2 faces is 4.

whyCorrect: \(\sin\theta\) is the vertical rise over the 82-inch brace, so the rise is \(82\left(\frac{9}{41}\right)=18\) inches. The horizontal distance is the remaining leg: \(\sqrt{82^{2}-18^{2}}=\sqrt{6724-324}=\sqrt{6400}=80\) inches. (The 9-40-41 triple doubled gives 18, 80, 82.)

whyWrong.A: 72 with a rise of 18 gives \(\sqrt{72^{2}+18^{2}}\) , about 74.2 inches, not an 82-inch brace.
whyWrong.B: 76 gives a brace of about 78.1 inches.
whyWrong.D: 84 is longer than the brace itself, which is impossible for a leg of the right triangle.

commonMistakes: Using \(\frac{9}{41}\) as the horizontal ratio; the sine always compares the opposite side, which here is the vertical rise.
tips: Recognising 9-40-41 turns the whole problem into doubling.

whyCorrect: Find each box's volume in cubic inches first: 48(24)(18) = 20,736 and 24(24)(12) = 6,912, which total 27,648 cubic inches. Dividing by 1,728 cubic inches per cubic foot gives 16 cubic feet.
commonMistakes: Converting each dimension to feet by dividing by 12 and then dividing the volume by 1,728 as well, which shrinks the answer by a factor of 1,728.
tips: Either work entirely in inches and convert once at the end, or convert every length first — never both.

whyCorrect: Each price multiplies the count it belongs to: the b horses shod all round bring 9 pence each, so 9b, and the f horses shod before only bring 4 pence each, so 4f. The day's takings are the sum, 9b + 4f.

whyWrong.B: 4b + 9f attaches each price to the wrong group of horses.
whyWrong.C: 13bf multiplies the two counts together, which corresponds to nothing here; it also adds the two prices as if every horse were charged both.
whyWrong.D: 13(b + f) charges every horse 13 pence, the two prices combined.

commonMistakes: Adding the two rates first; each rate applies only to its own group.
tips: Test with numbers: 2 horses all round and 1 before only should give 18 + 4 = 22 pence.

whyCorrect: N = 8s says s is multiplied by 8, so undo that by dividing both sides by 8: \(s=\frac{N}{8}\) .

whyWrong.A: s = 8N multiplies again instead of undoing the multiplication.
whyWrong.B: s = N - 8 undoes an addition, but nothing is added in N = 8s.
whyWrong.D: s = N + 8 makes the same mistake in the other direction.

commonMistakes: Treating the 8 as a term rather than a factor.
tips: Check with a number: 5 shoes need 40 nails, and 40/8 = 5.

whyCorrect: Divide both sides of 240 = 15h by 15: h = 240/15 = 16 hours.
commonMistakes: Multiplying 240 by 15, or subtracting 15.
tips: Check it back: 15(16) = 240 pounds of coal.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 12: the nails used are 45(12) = 540, so N = 900 - 540 = 360 nails left.

whyWrong.A: 300 subtracts 600, which would be a rate of 50 nails a day.
whyWrong.C: 420 subtracts 480 rather than 540.
whyWrong.D: 540 is the number of nails used, not the number left.

commonMistakes: Answering with the amount consumed instead of the amount remaining.
tips: Multiply before subtracting, and check that the answer is smaller than the 900 you started with.

whyCorrect: The rise per horse is the change in charge divided by the change in horses. From 2 horses to 5 the charge goes from 26 to 50, a rise of 24 shillings over 3 horses, so 24/3 = 8 shillings for each additional horse. The next rows agree: 74 - 50 = 24 over another 3 horses.

whyWrong.A: 4 would put the charge for 5 horses at 26 + 12 = 38 shillings.
whyWrong.B: 6 would give 26 + 18 = 44 shillings for 5 horses.
whyWrong.C: 7 would give 26 + 21 = 47 shillings, not the 50 in the table.

commonMistakes: Subtracting 50 - 26 and reporting 24 without dividing by the three extra horses.
tips: The table skips rows, so always divide the change in charge by the change in n.

whyCorrect: Solve the inequality: add 7 to both sides to get 4h > 28, then divide by 4 to get h > 7. The value must be strictly greater than 7, so 8 works.

whyWrong.A: 5 gives 4(5) - 7 = 13, which is not greater than 21.
whyWrong.B: 6 gives 17, still short.
whyWrong.C: 7 gives exactly 21, and the inequality is strict — 21 is not greater than 21.

commonMistakes: Treating > as ≥ and accepting the boundary value.
tips: Substitute the borderline choice into the original inequality; that is where these questions are decided.

whyCorrect: The cattle charge is 3 pence each, so 3h, and the pen adds a single 20 pence, giving a cost of 3h + 20. The drover cannot spend more than his 140 pence, so \(3h+20\le 140\) .

whyWrong.B: \(3h+20\ge 140\) says he must spend at least 140 pence, the reverse of a budget.
whyWrong.C: \(20h+3\le 140\) swaps the two prices, charging 20 pence per head and 3 pence for the pen.
whyWrong.D: \(3h-20\le 140\) subtracts the pen charge instead of adding it.

commonMistakes: Attaching the one-off charge to the variable and the per-item charge to nothing.
tips: Ask which cost repeats: the per-head charge takes the variable, the one-time charge stands alone.

whyCorrect: Both terms share 4, a and b, so the common factor is 4ab. Dividing gives \(\frac{8a^{2}b}{4ab}=2a\) and \(\frac{-12ab^{2}}{4ab}=-3b\) , so the allowance is \(4ab(2a-3b)\) .

whyWrong.A: \(4ab(2a+3b)\) expands to \(8a^{2}b+12ab^{2}\) , with the wrong sign in the middle.
whyWrong.C: \(4a^{2}b^{2}(2a-3b)\) takes out more of each variable than both terms share, giving \(8a^{3}b^{2}\) when expanded.
whyWrong.D: \(2ab(4a-6)\) expands to \(8a^{2}b-12ab\) , which is missing a factor of b in the second term.

commonMistakes: Taking out the highest power of a variable that appears in either term rather than the highest that appears in both.
tips: Expand your factored form back out; every term must match the original exactly.

whyCorrect: The area of a square is the side squared: \((x-5)^{2}=(x-5)(x-5)\) . Multiplying out gives \(x^{2}-5x-5x+25\) , which is \(x^{2}-10x+25\) .

whyWrong.A: \(x^{2}-25\) is \((x-5)(x+5)\) , a difference of squares, not a square.
whyWrong.B: \(x^{2}+25\) squares each term separately, which drops the middle term entirely.
whyWrong.C: \(x^{2}-5x+25\) counts the cross term once instead of twice.

commonMistakes: Squaring term by term; \((x-5)^{2}\) is not \(x^{2}-25\) .
tips: Test x = 7: the side is 2 and the area 4, and \(49-70+25=4\) .

whyCorrect: Substitute x = 0: \(f(0)=5(3)^{0}\) . Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1, so \(f(0)=5(1)=5\) lambs.

whyWrong.A: 0 comes from treating \(3^{0}\) as 0.
whyWrong.B: 3 reports the base rather than the value of the function.
whyWrong.D: 15 is 5(3), which is f(1), the count after one season.

commonMistakes: Reading the exponent 0 as making the whole expression 0.
tips: In \(f(x)=a\cdot b^{x}\) the coefficient a is always the starting value at x = 0.
